CPLMET-008.was: 16-18 km, and it is the coldest tropopause on earth
CPLMET-008.exp: Over the equator the tropopause sits at about 16-18 km, against about 8 km over the poles. The air keeps cooling with height all the way up to it, so the equatorial tropopause is the coldest on earth, about -75 to -80 °C, while the polar tropopause is only about -40 to -50 °C. 11 km at -56.5 °C is the ISA figure for the middle latitudes, not the equator's.
CPLMET-008.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLMET-046.exp: An isallobar joins places with the same pressure tendency, meaning the same change of pressure over the same period. A line joining places of equal pressure is an isobar, and temperature tendency has nothing to do with it. Isallobars show where pressure is falling or rising fastest, and so where a system is deepening or filling.
CPLMET-046.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLMET-258.exp: The peninsular discontinuity, also called the dry line, forms over peninsular India south of about 23°N in April and May, which is the pre-monsoon (hot weather) season. It separates hot, dry continental air from the north from cooler, moist air off the sea, and thunderstorms build along it. It is not a feature of the SW monsoon or of the NE monsoon.

CPLMET-296.exp: A single heat-type (air-mass) thunderstorm is most violent in its mature stage, when updraughts and downdraughts run side by side and the heaviest rain, hail, lightning and turbulence come. In the DGCA syllabus that stage is taken as lasting about 30 to 45 minutes. 2 hours and 3 to 4 hours are far too long for the violent phase of one cell; storms that last that long are clusters in which new cells keep forming. Some European manuals give a shorter mature stage, but for the DGCA paper the answer is 30 to 45 minutes.
CPLMET-296.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLMET-330.exp: Altostratus and nimbostratus are layer clouds holding a mix of supercooled water drops and ice crystals, and the icing to expect in them is light to moderate. Maximum icing belongs to towering cumulus and cumulonimbus, where large supercooled drops are concentrated. Negligible icing belongs to cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus, which are almost all ice crystals. Do not treat a thick nimbostratus as harmless: near a warm front its icing can become heavier.

CPLMET-357.exp: Over the poles the tropopause is only about 8 km up, and above it the temperature stops falling, staying around -40 to -50 °C. Over the equator the air keeps cooling right up to a tropopause at 16-18 km, where it reaches about -75 to -80 °C. So once you are above about 8 km, the coldest air is found over the equator, not over the poles.

CPLMET-378.exp: Drifting to starboard means the wind is blowing from your left (port) side. In the northern hemisphere, with your back to the wind the low pressure is on your left, and with the wind from the north that puts the low ahead of you, towards Calcutta. So you are flying from high towards low pressure. At a constant indicated altitude the aircraft follows the lowering pressure surface down, and true altitude is lower than indicated: high to low, look out below.

CPLMET-468.exp: The high-level clouds are cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus, found from about 16,500 ft (5 km) up to about 45,000 ft in temperate latitudes. They are made of ice crystals, so they carry no icing and no turbulence. Altostratus and altocumulus are medium-level clouds (nimbostratus is grouped with them although its base can be low), and stratus, stratocumulus and cumulus are low clouds.

CPLMET-478.exp: A SPECI is issued when the mean surface wind speed has changed by 10 kt or more from the last report. The other wind triggers are a change in the mean direction of 60° or more, with the mean speed 10 kt or more before or after the change, and an increase in the gusts of 10 kt or more, with the mean speed 15 kt or more before or after the change. Any one of them is enough to issue the report.
CPLMET-478.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLMET-480.exp: Below about 5,000 ft, take 30 ft for every hPa. An aerodrome that sits 30 hPa above the QNH datum, meaning its QFE is 30 hPa lower than its QNH, is therefore about 30 x 30 = 900 ft above mean sea level.

CPLMET-489.exp: Wingtip vortices get their strength from the aircraft's weight, wingspan, speed and configuration. They are strongest when a heavy aeroplane is flying slowly in a clean configuration, because it is then making a great deal of lift at a high angle of attack. More speed and extended flaps both reduce the strength of the vortex, which is why the other two choices are wrong.

CPLNAV-070.exp: A rate one turn is 3° a second, so 30 seconds gives 90° and the real heading reaches 135 + 90 = 225. In the northern hemisphere, turning through south makes the direct-reading compass lively: it runs ahead of the turn and over-reads. So when the aircraft is actually on 225, the compass shows more than 225. That is why you roll out late, overshooting the reading, when turning onto a southerly heading.
CPLNAV-070.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLNAV-178.was: slightly smaller (contracted) than the nominal scale, and larger outside them
CPLNAV-178.exp: On a Lambert conformal chart the scale is correct on the two standard parallels. Between them it is slightly too small (contracted), and smallest of all on the parallel of origin; outside them it is slightly too large (expanded). Placing the standard parallels about one sixth of the way in from the top and bottom of the chart keeps that variation small.
CPLNAV-178.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLNAV-209.exp: This is the tropical year, the length of one full cycle of the seasons: 365 days 5 hours 48 minutes 45 seconds (365 d 5 h 48.75 min). It is the year the calendar is kept in step with, by adding a leap day every fourth year. Measured against the distant stars, one orbit (the sidereal year) is a little longer, about 365 days 6 hours, but the answer the paper wants here is the tropical year.
CPLNAV-209.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLNAV-220.exp: Civil twilight lasts while the sun's centre is between 0°50' and 6° below the horizon, a fall of just over 5°. At the equator at the equinox the sun goes straight down at 15° an hour, which is 1° every 4 minutes, so this takes only about 21 to 24 minutes, the shortest twilight anywhere. At higher latitudes the sun sets at a slant and twilight lasts longer. Of the choices given, 24 minutes is the one that fits.
CPLNAV-220.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLNAV-259.exp: At 0930, when B departs, A is already 250 x 0.5 = 125 NM out. Five minutes before that, B is still 350 x 5/60 = about 29 NM short of the meeting point, roughly 408 NM out. Only the choice with 1045 and a meeting place of 437.5 NM fits.

CPLNAV-350.exp: Once a flight plan is filed, ATS expects you at the destination. If you divert and land where there is no ATS unit, tell ATS without delay, by the quickest means available, that you are down, and inform both the filed destination and the departure aerodrome. The 30-minute figure comes from search and rescue: if an aircraft has not arrived within 30 minutes of its ETA, ATS declares the uncertainty phase and starts alerting action. Report inside that window and you stop a search being started for an aircraft that is safely on the ground.
CPLNAV-350.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLNAV-365.exp: 5000 is the minimum en-route altitude (MEA): the lowest published altitude between the radio fixes that keeps you clear of obstacles across the whole width of the airway segment and, in many countries, also assures reception of the navigation aids that define it. CPLNAV-423.exp: Zero fuel mass is the dry operating mass plus the traffic load (passengers, baggage and cargo): everything except usable fuel. So 'ZFM = DOM + take-off fuel' is false, and that is the answer. Take-off mass is ZFM plus take-off fuel, which is true. Watch the third line as well: landing mass is take-off mass minus the TRIP fuel burnt, not minus the take-off fuel, so as printed it is also wrong. The statement the paper is after is the first one.
CPLNAV-423.note: As worded in the recall, two of the three statements are false: the third should read LM = TOM - trip fuel. The key gives the first statement, which is the one the paper is testing.

CPLNAV-504.was: 90 m (60 m + half wingspan); 600 m (900 m if track changes)
CPLNAV-504.exp: Obstacles count if they lie within 90 m plus 0.125 D either side of the take-off path, where D is the distance from the end of the TODA. CPLNAV-620.was: K x sqrt(temperature in kelvin) knots
CPLNAV-620.exp: The speed of sound depends only on the absolute temperature of the air: LSS = 38.95 x √T knots, with T in kelvin (°C + 273). At ISA sea level, 288 K, that gives about 661 kt; at -56.5 °C (216.5 K) it gives about 573 kt. A temperature in °C or °F cannot go under the root, because it must be absolute. The same law works in metres per second, but with a different constant, so the formula this question describes is the one in knots.
CPLNAV-620.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLNAV-713.exp: Raising the frequency of a sky wave means the ionosphere bends it less, so the critical angle grows and both the skip distance and the dead space increase. Those two statements are true. The untrue one is 'absorption increases': in the ionosphere, which is what matters for sky waves, a higher-frequency wave passes through with less absorption. That is why the highest frequency that still returns for a given range gives the strongest signal.
CPLNAV-713.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLNAV-737.was: the first sky wave to return to earth, at the critical angle - it defines the skip distance
CPLNAV-737.exp: Sky-wave angles are measured from the vertical. Rays sent up steeply, close to the vertical, pass through the ionosphere and are lost to space. As the angle from the vertical increases, a point is reached where the wave is bent enough to come back to earth: that is the critical angle, and this first returning sky wave (the critical ray) lands at the skip distance. Between the end of the surface wave and that point there is no signal, the dead space.
CPLNAV-737.why: Key right; old explanation found wrong by the independent check. New explanation written 2026-11-03 and checked against the source recorded in explanations-2026-11-03.json. Not yet independently audited.

CPLREG-039.was: 5 km flight visibility, 1500 m horizontally and 300 m (1000 ft) vertically from cloud
CPLREG-039.exp: Below 3,050 m (10,000 ft) AMSL and above 900 m (3,000 ft) AMSL, or 300 m above terrain, whichever is higher, VFR in classes B to G needs 5 km flight visibility and a distance from cloud of 1,500 m horizontally and 300 m (1,000 ft) vertically. At and above 10,000 ft the visibility rises to 8 km. At and below 3,000 ft in classes F and G, clear of cloud with the surface in sight is enough, and the authority may allow visibility down to 1,500 m for some flights.

CPLREG-153.exp: Hail needs strong updraughts that carry ice particles up and down through a deep layer of supercooled water, so they grow layer by layer until they are heavy enough to fall. Only a cumulonimbus has updraughts like that. Stratus gives drizzle, and nimbostratus gives continuous rain or snow, but neither can make hail.

CPLREG-022.exp: The Student Pilot’s Licence is valid for ten years. G.S.R. 289(E) of 8 April 2022 (the Aircraft (First Amendment) Rules, 2022) changed the SPL entry in the Rule 39C table from five years to ten; the 2023 amendment then raised the CPL and ATPL to ten as well.
